business_question: Without any labelled attack data, can we rank network connections so that the intrusions rise to the top of an analyst's alert queue?
success_criteria: PR-AUC many times the 3.4% attack base rate.
Useful precision within a realistic alert budget, not just in aggregate.
No detector may see a label during fitting.
Report which attack families remain invisible rather than only the average.

phases.title: 1. Business Understanding
phases.purpose: Translate a business question into a measurable data-mining goal and fix the success criteria before seeing any results.
phases.summary: Framed as triage, not classification. An analyst team has finite hours, so the product is a ranked queue and the metric that matters is what fraction of the first hundred alerts are real. Unsupervised methods were mandated because in a real deployment labelled intrusions do not exist until after the incident.
activities: Defined the deliverable as a ranked alert queue with a fixed budget.
Rejected accuracy outright given the 3.4% base rate.
Fixed the no-labels-in-fitting rule as a hard constraint.
Set contamination from an operational assumption, not the data.

findings.implication: PR-AUC and precision@k are the reported metrics.

decisions.decision: Set contamination to a stated 2% assumption.
decisions.rationale: In deployment the true rate is unknown; supplying it would leak the answer through a hyperparameter.
decisions.rejection_reason: Would flatter every detector and could not be reproduced in production.

phases.title: 2. Data Understanding
phases.purpose: Acquire the data, describe it honestly, and surface quality problems early enough that they can change the plan.
phases.summary: 80,000 connections, 39 features, 3.37% attacks spanning 10 named families.
activities: Profiled all numeric and categorical telemetry.
Measured univariate separability by Cohen's d.
Tabulated attack families and their prevalence.

findings.statement: Byte counts span nine orders of magnitude
findings.evidence: src_bytes ranges from 0 to hundreds of megabytes
findings.implication: Log transforms and a robust scaler are required before any distance-based method.

findings.statement: Attack families are extremely unbalanced among themselves
findings.evidence: 10 families, most with a handful of instances
findings.implication: Aggregate recall would hide entire rare classes; per-family recall is reported instead.

decisions.decision: Keep the label strictly out of the feature frame.
decisions.rationale: Removes any code path where a detector could see it.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Drop the label at fit time
decisions.rejection_reason: One forgotten column selection and the whole project silently becomes supervised.

phases.title: 3. Data Preparation
phases.purpose: Construct the modelling dataset: selection, cleaning, feature engineering and the train/test protocol that makes evaluation trustworthy.
phases.summary: RobustScaler on the numerics, one-hot on protocol/service/flag, log transforms on byte counts. Fitted once, on unlabelled data.
activities: Log-transformed source and destination byte counts.
Scaled numerics by median and IQR rather than mean and variance.
One-hot encoded the three categorical fields.

findings.evidence: mean and variance of src_bytes are set by the outliers themselves
findings.implication: RobustScaler used: median and IQR are unmoved by the very connections we are hunting.

decisions.rationale: Anomalies must stay far from the centre after scaling.
decisions.rejection_reason: Normalising by outlier-inflated variance shrinks exactly the deviations being detected.

phases.title: 4. Modeling
phases.purpose: Select techniques, search their hyperparameters, and record what was tried -- including what failed.
phases.summary: Five detectors with genuinely different definitions of 'anomalous', all fitted on identical features. Best single: Isolation Forest at PR-AUC 0.5056. Rank fusion did not beat it.
activities: Fitted Isolation Forest, LOF, One-Class SVM, Elliptic Envelope and PCA reconstruction.
Documented each detector's assumption and its blind spot.
Fused all five by rank averaging.
Simulated analyst alert budgets from 25 to 1,600.

findings.implication: Its isolation assumption fits telemetry where attacks are extreme on individual axes.

findings.statement: 3 of 4 detectors are INVERTED on this data
findings.evidence: ROC-AUC below 0.5 means they rank intrusions as more normal than benign traffic
findings.implication: The dominant DoS families are highly repetitive, so they form the densest regions of the space. Every density-based detector therefore treats the attacks as the most ordinary traffic present. This is the central lesson of the project: 'anomalous' and 'malicious' are not the same property, and a frequent attack is not an outlier.

findings.evidence: Elliptic Envelope: 15,325 of 80,000 scores were NaN or infinite
findings.implication: A detector that cannot produce finite scores on this feature matrix is a result about the method's assumptions, not a bug to be silently skipped.

findings.evidence: PR-AUC ranges 0.0275 to 0.5056 across five methods on identical features
findings.implication: 'Anomaly' is not one concept; the definition chosen determines what is found.
Deployed the single best detector; averaging in weaker detectors diluted the strong signal.

decisions.decision: Include Elliptic Envelope despite expecting it to lose.
decisions.rationale: A deliberately mis-specified Gaussian reference shows how much the distributional assumption costs.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Only run methods likely to win
decisions.rejection_reason: Removes the comparison that makes the others interpretable.

decisions.decision: Fuse by rank, not by raw score.
decisions.rationale: The five score scales are incomparable.
decisions.rejection_reason: Whichever detector has the largest numeric range would silently dominate.

criteria: Fusion evaluated rather than assumed to help

phases.title: 5. Evaluation
phases.purpose: Assess results against the business criteria from phase 1, not just the loss function, and review the whole process for defects.
phases.summary: Isolation Forest achieves PR-AUC 0.474 against a 0.034 base rate -- 14x random. In a 100-alert queue, 56% of alerts are real intrusions.
activities: Scored PR-AUC, ROC-AUC and precision at seven alert budgets.
Measured recall per attack family.
Compared against hand-written signature rules.
Projected the feature space to show where detection fails.

findings.evidence: PR-AUC 0.474 vs 0.254 for the best rule
findings.implication: Justifies the unsupervised approach over a rule sheet.

findings.statement: 5 attack families are invisible at a 400-alert budget
findings.implication: These intrusions look statistically normal; they require signature-based rules, not outlier detection. Reporting only the aggregate would have hidden this entirely.

findings.statement: Precision degrades as the alert budget grows
findings.implication: Directly sizes the analyst team required for a target recall.

decisions.decision: Report per-family recall, not just PR-AUC.
decisions.rationale: A strong average can coexist with one entire attack class never being surfaced.
decisions.rejection_reason: Would conceal the single most operationally important weakness.

phases.title: 6. Deployment
phases.purpose: Ship the model behind an interface, with monitoring, documented limits, and a plan for the day the data drifts.
phases.summary: Scored connections are served at /api/projects/anomaly/predict, returning a percentile-normalised anomaly score and the features that deviate most from normal.
activities: Pickled the fitted preprocessor and detector.
Exposed an alert-budget simulator for capacity planning.
Documented the families that require signature rules instead.

findings.statement: Scores are served as percentiles, not raw values
findings.evidence: raw isolation scores are uninterpretable on their own
findings.implication: An analyst can read 'top 0.5% most unusual' directly.

findings.statement: KDD-99 is a 1999 simulation, not modern traffic
findings.evidence: documented prominently in the model card
findings.implication: Results demonstrate methodology; they are not a claim about contemporary network security.

decisions.decision: Serve a percentile score plus deviating features.
decisions.rationale: An unexplained score cannot be triaged.
decisions.rejection_reason: Meaningless without the population it came from.

iteration_notes: The first run passed the observed attack rate as contamination and produced flattering numbers. The audit caught it as leakage through a hyperparameter, which is why contamination is now a stated 2% assumption.
Per-family recall was added after aggregate PR-AUC looked strong; it revealed that whole attack classes sit inside the normal density and cannot be found by any outlier method.
methodology: CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining), Chapman et al. 2000. Phases are iterative; the notes below record where this project looped back rather than proceeding linearly.
